newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Oil, Armenia seen in Azeri leader's Moscow talks.
newsitem.headline: Oil, Armenia seen in Azeri leader's Moscow talks.

text.p: Azeri President Haydar Aliyev began his first state visit to Russia on Wednesday, hoping to improve relations and seal a big oil deal but also to raise the thorny issue of Russian aid for his Armenian adversaries.
"I have high hopes for this visit," Aliyev told Interfax news agency on his arrival in Moscow.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Valery Serov told Interfax the two sides, whose relations have been strained in the past, would initial a new-look version of a friendship and cooperation treaty signed in 1992 after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

"This document contains important modifications which reflect new realities," said Serov, who is in charge of relations with other members of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), a loose body grouping most ex-Soviet republics.
"This accord has a solid base and I hope to be able to sign it," Aliyev said on arriving in Moscow.

"I also hope to sign several other documents which have direct reference to economic cooperation between our two countries," said Aliyev, who held talks with Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on his arrival in Moscow.
The treaty is due to be signed on Thursday in the presence of Russian President Boris Yeltsin.
Aliyev's office said on Tuesday that Azerbaijan and Russian oil giant LUKoil LKOH.RTS would sign a deal this week on joint development of the Yalama oil field in the Azeri sector of the Caspian Sea.
LUKoil President Vagit Alekperov said in Baku in May that the offshore field, about 200 km north of Baku in the Caspian, is estimated to contain at least 50 million tonnes of crude oil.
Aliyev's visit is also aimed at lifting the last obstacles to an accord on the transit of Azeri oil through Russia's breakaway Chechen republic to the Black Sea port of Novorossiisk.
Baku has accused Russia of lagging behind in implementing the deal on the pipeline, which is due to carry the first oil from an $8 billion international consortium by October.
Aliyev said he also planned to raise the issue of Russian arms supplies to Armenia, whose long-running conflict with Azerbaijan over the Nagorno-Karabakh region has yet to be finally resolved.

"We raised the issue of the transfer of Russian arms to the Armenian side during my visit to Moscow in March (during a summit of CIS leaders). Then we were told that an investigation was under way," Aliyev told Interfax.

"I would like to know what has been discovered and, mainly, we are raising the issue of the return of these weapons to Russia. In our view, the presence of such a large quantity of weaponry in Armenia right now presents a big danger," he said.
Aliyev said the Russian arms were worth $1 billion.
The issue of illegal transfers of arms to Armenia was first raised in February by Aman Tuleyev, then Russia's Minister for relations with CIS states.

Former defence minister Igor Rodionov confirmed that arms had been transferred, saying it had been done without the knowledge of the Russian leadership. The Russian prosecutor is investigating the reports.
